analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote to approve any major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The REINS Act, which would have let Congress block any federal rule costing the economy $100 million or more, died in a Senate committee with 29 cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how federal regulations work: any rule with an annual economic effect of $100 million or more could not take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed, and the President signed, a resolution approving it [S2] [S3]. If Congress did not act within 70 session days, the rule would be deemed dead [S2] [S3]. Because Congress rarely legislates that fast, the practical effect would have been to let any one veto point — either chamber, or the President — kill major health, safety, environmental, and financial rules [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing costly new federal rules would gain a powerful tool: any major rule could be stopped if either chamber of Congress declined to approve it or the President vetoed the approval [S3]. The bill's stated purpose is to increase accountability and transparency in the regulatory process by forcing Congress to vote on major rules [S2] [S3]. Regulated industries — energy, manufacturing, finance, and others — would gain the most, since rules with $100 million or more in annual economic effects cover the bulk of significant federal regulation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Gives regulated businesses a way to stop expensive new rules: any rule with an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or a major increase in costs or prices, would need an act of Congress before taking effect, and would simply die if Congress did not approve it within 70 session days.
Advances the bill's stated goal of making Congress accountable for the rules imposed on the public, by requiring a recorded vote on every major rule.
Guarantees expedited floor consideration for any approval resolution: committees must act within 15 session days or be discharged, and the Senate must hold a vote within 15 session days after that.

analysis.who_pays: The public would pay through weakened protections. Rules governing clean air and water, workplace safety, consumer finance, drug safety, and other areas often have economic effects of $100 million or more, and under the bill any of them could be killed by inaction in a single chamber or by a presidential veto [S3]. Federal agencies would also bear new reporting and classification duties for every rule [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill creates multiple points where a rule can be killed: if the House, the Senate, or the President fails to approve a major rule within 70 session days, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect — meaning Congress's routine inaction would kill most major rules by default.

A 70-session-day deadline is far shorter than the time Congress normally needs to pass any law, so complex technical rules on issues like air quality or financial safety would depend on rapid political agreement that rarely exists.

The bill carves out exceptions that complicate its own story: monetary policy rules are fully exempt, and rules covering things like specific rates, wages, and prices are excluded from the definition of a rule entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argue the bill restores the constitutional balance by making Congress own the major rules written in its name, and the expedited-vote machinery is genuinely well designed for that purpose [S3]. But the cost side is heavy: by requiring affirmative approval from both chambers plus the President for every major rule, it would have turned routine regulatory updates into full legislative battles, and the 70-day default of death would have allowed inaction anywhere in the system to block new protections [S2] [S3]. The burden would fall hardest on rules protecting public health, safety, and consumers, since those are exactly the rules with large economic effects.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee it was referred to never acted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on February 26, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day.
The bill attracted 29 cosponsors — 28 Republicans and one Democrat, Sen. Joe Manchin — but no vote was ever scheduled in the Senate.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing regulatory protections stayed in place, and federal agencies kept their authority to issue major rules. Businesses and industries that hoped to use Congress to block new rules gained nothing — but lost nothing either, since the rules in force before the bill remained in force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and existing regulatory protections

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 21 original cosponsors, framing it as restoring Congress's constitutional control over regulation.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the only Democrat among its 29 Senate supporters.

for.name: Senate Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a large Senate bloc behind it.

against.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup appears in the action history for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which had the power to schedule it once reported from committee.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the REINS approach and threatened to veto the House companion bill (H.R. 367) that passed the House in August 2013, signaling any approval pathway would face a presidential veto.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican — 28 of the 29 Senate cosponsors were Republicans, with Sen. Joe Manchin the lone Democrat — and no votes were ever taken to test it further.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, finance, and others)
industries.note: The bill would have handed these industries a veto over the rules that constrain them: any rule with $100 million or more in annual economic effects could be killed by inaction in a single chamber or a presidential veto [S3]. Their gain would come directly from weakened public health, safety, environmental, and financial protections.

Agencies would lose their ability to put major rules into effect without an act of Congress and would face new reporting and classification duties for every rule [S3]. Since these agencies write the protections ordinary people rely on, their loss would be the public's loss.
